node-1.label: Asymptomatic nodule on scalp for 3 months

node-2.label: Patient is a man in his 40s with no systemic complaints, no history of arthropod bite, immunosuppression, travel abroad, or contact with animals in the recent past

node-3.label: Physical examination revealed a skin-colored, firm, nontender, freely mobile 2 × 1.5-cm nodule with overlying normal skin on the right occipital region of the scalp; there was no lymphadenopathy and no other cutaneous lesions

why.why: The prior clinical impression of a benign subcutaneous tumor/cyst is directly contradicted by histopathological examination, which shows cross-sections of parasites with cuticular ridges, outer cuticle, muscle layer, and gravid uterus containing microfilariae, surrounded by a fibrous capsule and mixed inflammation. Both the pathologist and radiologist interpret this as diagnostic of parasitic infection, not a benign tumor/cyst. Therefore confidence is reduced from 0.8 to 0.05.

Histopathology revealing a parasitic filarial nodule is unanimously interpreted by the pathologist, radiologist, and laboratory physician as an infectious/inflammatory process. The negative peripheral blood smear does not exclude occult filariasis, and no benign tumoral or malignant features are present; benign tumor/cyst and malignancy are effectively ruled out by the same histopathological evidence. Confidence remains 0.95.

Histopathological examination reveals a parasitic inflammatory nodule with no malignant features; the pathologist and radiologist both confirm a non-neoplastic infectious process. This further refutes malignant neoplasm, lowering confidence from 0.1 to 0.05.

node-7.label: Histopathology shows parasite cross-sections with cuticular ridges, outer cuticle, muscle layer, and gravid uterus containing microfilariae, surrounded by fibrous capsule and mixed inflammation

node-8.label: The scalp nodule is a parasitic infection (e.g., filarial nodule)

why.why: Histopathology is definitive: parasite cross-sections with cuticular ridges, muscle layer, and a gravid uterus containing microfilariae, surrounded by fibrous capsule and mixed inflammation. The pathologist, radiologist, and laboratory physician all independently confirm this as a filarial nodule. The negative peripheral blood smear does not exclude occult filariasis, and although serology and ultrasound are unavailable (limiting species identification), the diagnosis of a filarial nodule remains highly confident.

node-9.label: Peripheral blood smear was negative for microfilariae

node-10.label: Serological testing for filariasis was not performed (unavailable)

node-11.label: Ultrasound examination of the nodule was not performed (unavailable)

node-12.label: The scalp nodule is an occult filarial infection (microfilariae present in tissue but absent from peripheral blood)

attrs.why: Histopathology demonstrates microfilariae within the gravid uterus of the parasite in the nodule, while the peripheral blood smear is negative. The laboratory physician explicitly notes that a negative blood smear does not exclude occult filariasis. This combination—tissue microfilariae without peripheral blood microfilariae—defines occult filariasis and refines the diagnosis of filarial nodule, although species identification remains limited by unavailable serology and ultrasound.
